_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. status: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship / corroborated by reference works, citation in note), 'decided' (project style call, e.g. standard pinyin or a fixed convention), 'provisional' (a romanization of mine not found attested; the builder appends a visible marker). Sections render as glossary headings; keys starting with '_' are ignored.

黄慕兰.note: The author. Name taken in 1926 on joining the revolution (慕兰, ‘admiring Mulan’); the book’s title form.

黄彰定.note: The author’s birth and school name; style name Shuyi (淑仪). Corroborated by Chinese biographies.

黄定慧.note: A later name the author adopted in 1932; the form under which she is widely cited and by which the book’s photographs caption her.

谭嗣同.note: 1865–1898; Liuyang reformer, one of the ‘Six Gentlemen’ of 1898.

唐才常.note: 1867–1900; Liuyang reformer, with Tan Sitong the ‘Two Heroes of Liuyang.’

欧阳中鹄.note: 1849–1911; Liuyang Confucian scholar, teacher of Tan and Tang.

詹天佑.note: 1861–1919 (Jeme Tien Yow); pioneering railway engineer of the Beijing–Zhangjiakou line.

花木兰.note: Legendary woman warrior of the ‘Ballad of Mulan’; source of the author’s name.

何香凝.note: Wife of Liao Zhongkai; Kuomintang left-wing leader.

陈潭秋.note: 1896–1943; CCP founding member; the author’s leader in the Jiangxi underground.

杜韫章.note: Original name of Zhang Yun (章蕴, 1905–1995); the source glosses the identity inline.

李子芬.note: Standard pinyin; the CYL organizer who recruited the author.

袁溥之.note: d. 1994; Northern Expedition comrade of the author.

张笃和.note: Standard pinyin of a comrade of the author’s Wuhan years.

周恩来.note: 1898–1976; then the real director of the Party’s underground work in Shanghai; the author’s superior.

陈独秀.note: 1879–1942; first general secretary of the CCP, removed at the August Seventh Conference of 1927.

李一纯.note: Wife of Li Lisan; standard pinyin.

贺昌.note: 1906–1935; the author’s second husband; killed covering the Long March rearguard.

饶漱石.note: 1903–1975; later condemned in the 1954 Gao–Rao affair.

向忠发.note: 1880–1931; figurehead general secretary of the CCP from 1928.

吴德峰.note: Director of the Central Liaison Bureau.

徐虔直.note: Wife of Chen Tanqiu; romanization of 徐虑直 not found attested.

谢冰莹.note: 1906–2000; writer, author of Diary of a Woman Soldier; Whampoa 6th-class woman cadet.

胡兰畦.note: 1901–1994; writer, author of In Prison; Whampoa 6th-class woman cadet.

陈友仁.note: 1878–1944; foreign minister of the Wuhan Nationalist government; conventional English form retained.

孙传芳.note: Warlord of the five southeastern provinces.

鲍罗廷.note: Mikhail Borodin (1884–1951), Comintern adviser to the Kuomintang at Wuhan.

沈定一.note: 1883–1928; early Communist; father of Shen Jianlong.

沈剑龙.note: First husband of Yang Zhihua; son of Shen Dingyi.

夏斗寅.note: Northern Expedition officer who mutinied against the Communists in May 1927.

许克祥.note: Launched the Changsha “Horse Day” coup, 21 May 1927.

耿丹.note: Styled Zhongzhao; deputy commander of the 15th Army; husband of Zhang Duhe.

赵畹华.note: Standard pinyin; the author’s Wuhan-years comrade.

汪华贞.note: Director of the Institute for Reforming New People at Wuhan.

刘少文.note: Subject of Appendix III; interpreter at the 1927 Wuhan reception.

江一平.note: Prominent Shanghai lawyer of the 1920s–30s; son-in-law of the magnate Yu Qiaqing. Assigned as the author’s duty defense lawyer in her 1929 mill-strike trial.

虞洽卿.note: Powerful Ningbo-born comprador and business magnate of Republican Shanghai.

李维汉.note: Alias Luo Mai (罗迈). Central Committee member and secretary of the Jiangsu Provincial Committee about 1929; a senior Party organizer.

王明.note: Chen Shaoyu; leader of the Moscow-trained ‘28 Bolsheviks’ and of the third ‘Left’ line (1931–35). Here still an obscure Red Flag reporter.

夏征农.note: Veteran Communist and writer; a member of the Central Advisory Commission in the 1980s.

聂荣臻.note: Later a marshal of the People’s Republic; in 1929–30 in charge of military work under the Guangdong Provincial Committee / Southern Bureau.

柯麟.note: Communist doctor who ran a Shanghai clinic (the Dasheng Clinic) as an underground liaison cover.

李强.note: Builder of the Party’s first wireless sets and secret radio stations; later PRC Minister of Foreign Trade.

张瑞华.note: Nie Rongzhen’s wife and a Party worker.

熊瑾玎.note: Manager of the Party Central’s clandestine finances in Shanghai.

贺平.note: The author’s second son, by He Chang, born March 1930 in Hong Kong; given to Lu Biao to raise and renamed Lu Ziping, later Lu Ping (卢平).

卢彪.note: Successor to He Chang as Southern Bureau (Guangdong Provincial Committee) secretary; adoptive father of the author’s son He Ping.

何葆贞.note: Liu Shaoqi’s wife (also written He Baozhen / He Bao’e), a Party worker and the author’s former Wuhan colleague; martyred 1934.

彭真.note: Later a top Party leader and mayor of Beijing; here Tianjin municipal committee secretary, arrested about this time.

薄一波.note: Later a vice-premier and Party elder; here Beiping municipal committee secretary.

陈复.note: A Northern Bureau leader arrested with the failed 1930 insurrections. The memoir calls him propaganda head; scholarship makes him the Bureau’s secretary-general.

任弼时.note: A principal Party and Youth League leader, later one of the ‘Five Secretaries’ of the Central Secretariat.

米夫.note: Pavel Mif, Comintern representative who engineered the Fourth Plenum of January 1931 that raised Wang Ming.

秦邦宪.note: Better known as Bo Gu (博古); one of the ‘28 Bolsheviks’ and de facto Party leader 1931–35.

张闻天.note: Alias Luo Fu (洛甫); a ‘28 Bolshevik’ who became general secretary after the Zunyi Conference.

王稼祥.note: Party and military leader; a supporter of Mao at the Zunyi Conference.

陈毅.note: Later a marshal and foreign minister of the People’s Republic.

毛泽覃.note: Mao Zedong’s youngest brother; killed in 1935.

戴晓云.note: New secretary of the Mutual Aid General Association from the winter of 1930; romanization by pinyin.

陈赓.note: Whampoa graduate and head of the intelligence (2nd) section of the Party’s Special Branch; later a PLA general.

谭延闿.note: Hunan military governor and Nationalist elder; first president of the Executive Yuan; signed the Wuhan order expelling Chiang in April 1927.

黄兴.note: Revolutionary leader and Sun Yat-sen’s chief military partner in the 1911 Revolution.

蔡锷.note: Republican general who led the 1915–16 revolt against Yuan Shikai’s monarchy.

顾顺章.note: Head of the Party’s Special Branch whose 1931 defection to the Kuomintang gravely wrecked the Shanghai underground.

戚元德.note: Wu Defeng’s wife and a Party worker skilled at persuasion; she talked the author into staying in Shanghai.

黄浩.note: Also styled Jingwen (静汰); staff officer of the Rescue Department, formerly of the Whampoa women’s corps. Romanization by pinyin.

朱伯琛.note: Secretary of the Mutual Aid General Association; son of Zhu Jianfan, headmaster of the Zhounan Girls’ School. Romanization by pinyin.

陈志皋.note: Progressive Shanghai lawyer of the Haining Chen clan; recruited to defend arrested Communists, he later became the author’s husband.

陈元龙.note: The ‘Grand Councilor Chen’ of the Kangxi–Yongzheng era, ancestor of the Haining Chen clan.

陈其寿.note: Styled Jieqing (介卿); Chen Zhigao’s father, a retired judge of the criminal court of the Shanghai French Concession’s Mixed Court; the author’s adoptive father.

翁同龢.note: The Guangxu Emperor’s tutor, cashiered in 1898 during the Hundred Days’ Reform.

黄金荣.note: Green Gang boss and the sole Chinese chief inspector of the French Concession patrol house; Chiang Kai-shek was once his disciple.

沈钧儒.note: Jurist and patriotic democrat, later one of the ‘Seven Gentlemen’; Chen Zhigao’s teacher and elder cousin.

褚辅成.note: Patriotic democrat and educator, principal of the Shanghai College of Law.

施蛰存.note: Modernist writer and scholar; a schoolmate bailed out by Chen’s father.

戴望舒.note: Celebrated modernist poet (‘Rainy Alley’); a schoolmate bailed out by Chen’s father.

杜衡.note: Writer and critic (Su Wen); a schoolmate bailed out by Chen’s father.

周康文.note: CCP Central Propaganda Department cadre who organized the World and China Society.

孙晓村.note: Economist and democrat; later a vice-chairman of the CPPCC and of the China Democratic National Construction Association.

钱纳水.note: Head of the propaganda department of the Mutual Aid General Association. Romanization by pinyin.

赵韵逸.note: The young judge who tried Guan Xiangying’s case. Romanization by pinyin.

贝淞生.note: Manager of the Bank of China and a sworn friend of the elder Chen. Romanization by pinyin.

宛希先.note: Cousin of the author’s first husband Wan Xiyan; an early Jinggangshan leader wrongly killed in the anti-‘AB-tuan’ purge about 1930.

邓榕.note: Pen name Maomao (毛毛); Deng Xiaoping’s daughter and biographer.

曹炳生.note: A French-Concession Municipal Police interpreter, classmate and dormitory-mate of Chen Zhigao at Xuhui College; his unwitting talk of Xiang Zhongfa’s arrest tipped off the author. Assassinated early in the War of Resistance.

薛耕莘.note: A Chinese detective in the Shanghai French-Concession police who succeeded to Cao Bingsheng’s post; later a research fellow of the Shanghai Research Institute of Culture and History and a memoirist (1901–2007).

孙雪影.note: Cao Bingsheng’s widow, headmistress of the Bingsheng Primary School founded in his memory.

康生.note: Took charge of the Central Special Branch after Gu Shunzhang’s defection in 1931; later a Politburo member and a chief instigator of the Cultural Revolution (1898–1975).

王震.note: Red Army and PLA general, later Vice-President of the PRC (1908–1993).

张国焘.note: An early CCP leader who, during the Long March, split with the Central Committee over the line of march; later defected to the Kuomintang (1897–1979).

柳亚子.note: Poet and founder of the Southern Society (Nanshe); a friend of Chen Zhigao’s (1887–1958).

李一氓.note: Party veteran and writer; the author quotes his account of the ‘Wu Hao’ affair from the volume Pan Hannian in Shanghai (1903–1990).

董竹君.note: Founder of the Jinjiang restaurant and hotel in Shanghai and author of the memoir My One Century; earlier the wife of Xia Zhishi (1900–1997).

夏之时.note: A Sichuan military commander (‘Commander Xia’, 都督) of the 1911 Revolution era; Dong Zhujun’s first husband, from whom she was divorced (1887–1950).

吴湄.note: Proprietress of the Meilongzhen Restaurant in Shanghai.

文崇石.note: Author of an article in the New York Chinese-language paper Overseas Chinese Daily exposing the Gang of Four’s use of the ‘Wu Hao’ notices against Zhou Enlai.

张承宗.note: Head of the United Front Work Department of the CCP Shanghai Municipal Committee (1907–1991).

俞同芳.note: A noted Shanghai practitioner of Chinese medicine, called in to attend Chen Qishou.

陈宝璋.note: Chen Zhigao’s younger sister, then a student at the Sino-French College of Pharmacy.

陈寅谷.note: A younger brother of Chen Zhigao, a student at the Tongde Medical College who did battlefield relief in the 1932 fighting.

陈石君.note: A younger brother of Chen Zhigao, a student at the Tongde Medical College who did battlefield relief in the 1932 fighting.

陈胜年.note: Later named Peng Qing (彭清); a grandson of Chen Qishou, born just before the old man’s death.

巴和.note: A French lawyer in Shanghai, an old friend of Chen Qishou; he placed the counter-notice on behalf of ‘Zhou Shaoshan’. Chinese sources give only 倩和 (Baho); his name’s French original is not established.

周少山.note: A cover name of Zhou Enlai, used in the March 1932 counter-notice: the notice styled ‘Wu Hao’ as merely a former pen name of the private citizen ‘Zhou Shaoshan’, so that the ‘Wu Hao’ of the fake notice must be someone else.

刘伯垂.note: A veteran CCP politics-and-law expert; from 1933 he succeeded Pan Hannian as the author’s superior and contact for the Shanghai rescue and united-front work.

林庚白.note: 1897–1941; Southern Society poet and Nationalist-government legislator, once secretary-general of the Extraordinary Parliament; a friend and legal ally of the author and Chen Zhigao. Killed by the Japanese at Hong Kong in 1941.

杨志豪.note: A Shanghai lawyer and colleague of Chen Zhigao and Shen Junru in the Bar Association and the wrongful-imprisonment-compensation movement.

周孝庵.note: A Shanghai journalist and lawyer who ran a law office jointly with Chen Zhigao.

廖承志.note: 1908–1983; son of Liao Zhongkai and He Xiangning, CCP leader; arrested in Shanghai in 1933 and among those the author’s circle worked to rescue.

吴凯声.note: A prominent Shanghai barrister (trained in France) entrusted, behind the scenes, with the defense of Chen Geng and Liao Chengzhi.

何叔衡.note: 1876–1935; a delegate to the First Congress of the CCP; killed in 1935. His daughters He Shishan and He Sisi survived to witness the author’s rescue work.

何实山.note: Elder daughter of the martyr He Shuheng.

何实嗣.note: Younger daughter of He Shuheng; later director of the Beijing Research Institute of Culture and History.

朱端绶.note: Underground CCP worker; wife and working partner of Xiong Jinding; survived into the 1980s.

陈琮英.note: Wife of Ren Bishi; implicated and arrested after Xiang Zhongfa’s betrayal wrecked the Red Flag printing house.

蔡元培.note: 1868–1940; educator, first minister of education of the Republic, chancellor of Peking University, and head of Academia Sinica; a witness at the author’s 1935 wedding.

陈丕显.note: 1916–1995; CCP leader who fought in the south Jiangxi guerrilla war and wrote reminiscences of He Chang.

项英.note: 1898–1941; head of the CCP Central Soviet Area Sub-bureau left behind after the Long March; later political commissar of the New Fourth Army.

阮啸仙.note: 1898–1935; first director of the CCP’s Central Auditing Commission; killed in the south Jiangxi breakout, mourned with He Chang in Chen Yi’s poem.

李锐.note: 1917–2019; once a secretary to Mao Zedong, later deputy head of the Central Organization Department and a member of the Central Advisory Commission.

俞樾.note: 1821–1907; styled Quyuan; eminent Qing scholar of classical learning. The Yu Mansion by West Lake was built for him.

俞陛云.note: 1868–1950; grandson of Yu Yue and father of Yu Pingbo; a late-Qing tanhua (third-place palace-examination graduate) and Hanlin poet, style name Jieqing. He taught the author classical poetry at the Yu Mansion.

俞平伯.note: 1900–1990; son of Yu Biyun, poet and famous scholar of Dream of the Red Chamber (a ‘Redologist’).

曾国藩.note: 1811–1872; late-Qing statesman and general who funded the building of the Yu Mansion for Yu Yue.

吴梅村.note: Wu Weiye (1609–1672), late-Ming/early-Qing poet; his ‘Song of Chen Yuanyuan’ is quoted in this chapter.

陈圆圆.note: Famous courtesan of the Ming-Qing transition, subject of Wu Meicun’s poem.

高志航.note: 1907–1937; Nationalist air-force hero of the 14 August 1937 air battle over Hangzhou; killed later that year.

章士钊.note: 1881–1973; noted jurist, scholar and politician; a Beiping creditor of the Tongyi Company.

罗家衡.note: A lawyer and Jiangxi man; a Beiping creditor of the Tongyi Company and part of Wu Defeng’s social network.

张东荪.note: 1886–1973; philosopher and National Socialist Party figure, professor at Peking University.

杜月笙.note: 1888–1951; Green Gang boss and Shanghai power broker, invited to guarantee the Tongyi Company’s resumption.

王晓籁.note: 1887–1967; Shanghai business leader who became chairman of the revived Tongyi Company.

黄溯初.note: Pioneering banker; chairman of the Tongyi Trust Company, who fled to Japan after its 1935 collapse.

郭虞裳.note: England-trained founder of the Tongyi Company and a relative by marriage of Chen Zhigao’s eldest brother.

徐寄庼.note: Shanghai banker; managing director of the Tongyi Company who arranged the mortgage that let it resume business.

阿英.note: Pen name of Qian Xingcun (1900–1977), writer and literary historian; ran the ‘Wind and Rain Bookroom’ hidden in the Tongyi Company.

夏衍.note: 1900–1995; playwright, film-maker and CCP cultural cadre in Shanghai.

冯雪峰.note: 1903–1976; poet, literary theorist and CCP cultural figure, liaison to Shanghai’s writers.

方志敏.note: 1899–1935; CCP leader of the Northeast Jiangxi soviet; his prison diary was among the papers kept in the Tongyi vault.

陈云.note: 1905–1995; senior CCP leader; his later appraisal cleared the author of the ‘bureaucratic capitalist’ charge.

孙科.note: 1891–1973; son of Sun Yat-sen and a president of one of the Nationalist government’s Five Yuan.

于右任.note: 1879–1964; Nationalist elder statesman, calligrapher, and president of the Control Yuan.

张知本.note: 1881–1976; jurist and Nationalist elder; an introducer at the Lin Gengbai–Lin Beili betrothal.

覃振.note: 1885–1947; Nationalist elder statesman and Yuan president.

陈立夫.note: 1900–2001; Nationalist organization boss of the ‘CC Clique,’ firmly anti-Communist.

冯玉祥.note: 1882–1948; the ‘Christian General’ and warlord, at this time an anti-Japanese figure.

杜重远.note: 1898–1943; patriotic industrialist and editor of New Life Weekly, jailed in the 1935 ‘New Life’ case.

郑毓秀.note: 1891–1959; France-trained jurist, Shanghai’s first woman lawyer, qualified to plead in the Mixed Court.

李辛阳.note: Aurora University classmate of Chen Zhigao’s circle; assistant lawyer in Zheng Yuxiu’s office.

陈德新.note: Style name Mingzai; cousin of Chen Zhigao and chairman of the Zhejiang Provincial Bar Association.

张以璘.note: A CCP member (joined 1926) placed by Wu Defeng as secretary of Chen Zhigao’s law office, running it as a covert liaison point.

郭长禄.note: Wuhan University politics-and-diplomacy student who married the author’s second sister.

于伶.note: 1907–1997; playwright and head of the Shanghai Drama Art Society, aided through Tongyi overdrafts.

申石伽.note: 1906–2001; noted Shanghai traditional-ink painter; the author studied painting under him at the Yu Mansion.

蒋雪英.note: Daughter of the maid in Madame Yu’s dowry; later Yu Pingbo’s goddaughter and pupil.

冒鹤亭.note: Mao Guangsheng (1873–1959), noted Jiangnan poet under whom the author later studied verse.

潘肇邦.note: Style name Luyan; senior Aurora University alumnus and accountant, co-mediator and later general manager of the revived Tongyi Company.

陈高佣.note: 1902–1976; historian and Jinan University professor, editor of The World and China; arrested in 1932.

程仲文.note: Student of Chen Gaoyong and proofreader for The World and China, arrested with him.

陈振九.note: Cousin of Chen Zhigao and a deputy manager of the Yongye Bank; guarantor for the released Chen Gaoyong.

陈赓虞.note: Chen Zhigao’s eldest brother; involved in the Yongchang Gold Exchange.

李焕之.note: Younger brother of Li Nanxiang; became Chen Lifu’s secretary, giving the author’s circle a source inside the Nationalist center. Not the composer of the same name.

武振东.note: Daxia University classmate of Li Huanzhi and member of the World and China Society.

潘震亚.note: A Jiangxi man whose social network helped place Zhang Yilin in Chen Zhigao’s office.

唐有壬.note: 1894–1935; diplomat and vice-minister of foreign affairs; an introducer at the author’s wedding, assassinated later that year.

吴羹梅.note: 1906–1991; industrialist known as China’s ‘pencil king,’ a wedding guest.

吴开先.note: 1899–1990; Nationalist ‘CC Clique’ figure and head of Shanghai’s Bureau of Social Affairs, lobbied to re-legalize the Southern Society.

陈霆锐.note: A famous Shanghai lawyer active in the wrongful-imprisonment-compensation movement.

陆鼎揆.note: A Shanghai lawyer active in the wrongful-imprisonment-compensation movement.

陈炯明.note: 1878–1933; Guangdong warlord who broke with Sun Yat-sen in 1922, cited in He Xiangning’s amnesty appeal.

林北丽.note: Woman poet; wife of Lin Gengbai and a lifelong friend of the author.

徐蕴华.note: Mother of Lin Beili; in the early Republic she helped mourn and bury the martyr Qiu Jin.

徐自华.note: 1873–1935; poet and friend of Qiu Jin who arranged her burial; elder sister of Xu Yunhua.

吴芝瑛.note: 1867–1934; calligrapher who, with Xu Zihua, braved danger to bury Qiu Jin.

李慕兰.note: An overseas-Chinese art student who happened to share the author’s name and lodged with her at the Yu Mansion.

胡伟克.note: Overseas-Chinese instructor at the Nationalist aviation school who married Li Mulan.

许宝.note: Nephew of Madame Yu; the source gives the name as ‘Xu Bao,’ which may be incomplete.

潘太夫人.note: Chen Zhigao’s mother, the author’s adoptive mother-in-law.

杨杏佛.note: Yang Quan (1893–1933); secretary-general of the China League for the Protection of Civil Rights, assassinated 1933.

马相伯.note: 1840–1939; Catholic educator, founder of Aurora and Fudan universities, patriotic elder of the salvation movement.

邹韬奋.note: 1895–1944; journalist and publisher of Life Weekly, one of the Seven Gentlemen.

章乃器.note: 1897–1977; banker-economist, one of the Seven Gentlemen.

李公朴.note: 1902–1946; educator, one of the Seven Gentlemen; assassinated at Kunming in 1946.

王造时.note: 1903–1971; scholar, one of the Seven Gentlemen.

沙千里.note: 1901–1982; lawyer, one of the Seven Gentlemen.

史良.note: 1900–1985; lawyer, the only woman of the Seven Gentlemen; first Minister of Justice of the PRC.

钱新之.note: Qian Yongming (1885–1958); Shanghai banker, a leading figure of the city’s financial world.

潘公展.note: 1894–1975; Kuomintang publicist and Shanghai municipal official.

蔡叔厚.note: 1898–1984; CCP underground figure connected to the World and China Society.

李南香.note: A Kuomintang provincial-party figure cooperating in united-front and intelligence work; romanization provisional.

金学成.note: A figure in the Shanghai salvation bodies linked to the Party; romanization provisional.

许广平.note: 1898–1968; educator and writer, wife of Lu Xun; editor of his Complete Works.

沈兹九.note: 1898–1989; women’s-movement leader and editor, one of the four ‘democratic big sisters.’

胡子婴.note: 1907–1982; women’s-movement figure, one of the four ‘democratic big sisters.’

宋美龄.note: 1898–2003; Madame Chiang Kai-shek, youngest of the Soong sisters.

李广安.note: Head of the Twenty-Ninth Army’s Shanghai liaison office; romanization provisional.

王孝英.note: A Kuomintang legislator on the Women’s Comfort Association board; romanization provisional.

谢祖仪.note: General secretary of the Shanghai Young Women’s Christian Association; romanization provisional.

刘王立明.note: 1897–1970; temperance and women’s-rights activist, head of the Chinese Women’s Temperance Union.

李秋君.note: 1899–1973; woman painter, president of the Women’s Painting and Calligraphy Association, disciple of Zhang Daqian.

高静宜.note: Wife of the businessman Wu Gengmei; a founder of the Chinese Women’s Vocational School; romanization provisional.

廖梦醒.note: 1904–1988; daughter of Liao Zhongkai and He Xiangning; secretary of the Women’s Comfort Association.

罗叔章.note: 1898–1992; women’s-movement leader and CCP member, one of the four ‘democratic big sisters.’

戚逸影.note: Principal of the Daren Primary School, deputy head of the Women’s Comfort Association’s comfort section; romanization provisional.

宋霭龄.note: 1889–1973; eldest of the Soong sisters, wife of Kong Xiangxi.

姚潜修.note: Student of Guo Moruo, leader of the southbound propaganda team, deputy general secretary of the International Relief shelter; romanization provisional.

林林.note: 1910–2011; poet and translator, student of Guo Moruo.

于立群.note: 1916–1979; calligrapher, later the wife of Guo Moruo.

钱亦石.note: 1889–1938 (style Jiepan); CCP theorist and educator; died of illness contracted at the front, called the first cultural worker to give his life for the resistance.

程潜.note: 1882–1968; Kuomintang general, later went over to the Communists.

杨应彬.note: A Guangdong CCP figure who as a young man went to the front with Qian Yishi’s cultural team; romanization provisional.

冼星海.note: 1905–1945; composer of the Yellow River Cantata; son-in-law of Qian Yishi.

韩长发.note: The author’s family chauffeur, who drove comfort goods to the front; romanization provisional.

田汉.note: 1898–1968; playwright and lyricist, author of the words of the PRC national anthem.

梁红玉.note: d. c. 1135; woman general of the Southern Song, wife of Han Shizhong; a patriotic heroine of a wartime opera.

韩世忠.note: 1090–1151; Southern Song general who resisted the Jin invasion.

张大千.note: 1899–1983; one of the most celebrated modern Chinese painters.

刘海粟.note: 1896–1994; painter and art educator, founder of the Shanghai Art Academy.

毛王瑞竹.note: A co-founder, with Li Qiujun and Qi Yiying, of a home for disaster orphans; romanization provisional.

饶家驹.note: Robert Jacquinot de Besange (1878–1946); French Jesuit, the ‘One-Armed Father,’ founder of the Nanshi Refugee Zone (the ‘Jacquinot Safe Zone’).

颜惠庆.note: W. W. Yen (1877–1950); diplomat and statesman, Chinese president of the International Relief Association.

潘达.note: Style Dacheng; an Aurora University student from Vietnam, deputy general secretary of the International Relief shelter; romanization provisional.

徐克强.note: Head of the production section of the International Relief shelter; romanization provisional.

赵朴初.note: 1907–2000; Buddhist leader, poet and calligrapher; later president of the Buddhist Association of China.

谌小岑.note: 1897–1992; an early Awakening Society member, later a Kuomintang official.

黄涵之.note: Maternal uncle of Zhao Puchu and a head of the Charity Federation; romanization provisional.

李祖虞.note: A lawyer whose wife organized the benefit performance in aid of Suiyuan; romanization provisional.

彭文应.note: 1904–1962; a leader of the salvation movement who joined Song Qingling’s ‘imprisonment’ petition.

胡愈之.note: 1896–1986; writer, publisher and Esperantist; member of the Fu She.

张志让.note: 1893–1978; jurist, later a vice-president of the Supreme People’s Court.

马占山.note: 1885–1950; general who led armed resistance against Japan in Manchuria in 1931–32.

陈秉璋.note: The author’s sister-in-law (Chen Zhigao’s sister), with whom she performed in an amateur benefit opera; romanization provisional.

曹亮.note: A comrade who, cherishing Zhou Enlai’s letter, renamed himself Rubi (‘precious jade’); romanization provisional.

黄镇.note: 1909–1989; painter and, later, diplomat; his Long March sketches were published as Sketches of the Westward Journey.

魏如晦.note: A pen name of A Ying (Qian Xingcun), devised by Yu Ling from the phrase ‘wind and rain, dark as nightfall.’

陈宜郁.note: Chen Zhigao’s niece, an underground courier to the New Fourth Army; later an army-level political commissar, killed in the civil war; romanization provisional.

李益.note: An underground courier who, with Chen Yiyu, carried Documents to the New Fourth Army; romanization provisional.

梅益.note: 1914–2003 (formerly Mei Yu); translator of How the Steel Was Tempered; later director of the Central Broadcasting Administration and editor-in-chief of the Encyclopedia of China Publishing House.

赵邦鑅.note: Manager of the Translation Herald and former manager of the Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury; romanization provisional.

扬帆.note: 1912–1999; CCP security and intelligence figure, later implicated with Pan Hannian.

王任叔.note: 1901–1972; writer (pen name Ba Ren) and, later, PRC ambassador to Indonesia.

姜椿芳.note: 1912–1987; translator, later a founder of the Encyclopedia of China.

韦悫.note: 1896–1976; educator and philosopher, later a deputy mayor of Shanghai.

孙特士·斐士.note: A British principal of the University Book Company, nominal publisher of the Daily Translation Herald; the English name is a provisional reconstruction (source: 孙特士·斗士).

拿门·鲍纳.note: A British principal of the University Book Company, nominal publisher of the Daily Translation Herald; the English name is a provisional reconstruction (source: 拿门·鲍纳).

张宗麟.note: 1899–1976; educator, disciple of Tao Xingzhi, CCP member and a convener of the Tuesday Dining Club.

胡咏淇.note: An industrial-commercial member of the Tuesday Dining Club; romanization provisional.

杨怀生.note: General secretary of the YMCA who kept the Tuesday Dining Club’s membership roll; romanization provisional.

刘湛恩.note: 1896–1938; first Chinese president of the University of Shanghai; assassinated by pro-Japanese agents in 1938.

陈鹤琴.note: 1892–1982; pioneering early-childhood educator; ran the Shanghai newsboys’ school.

沈体兰.note: 1899–1969; educator, member of the Tuesday Dining Club.

陈巳生.note: An industrial-commercial member of the Tuesday Dining Club; romanization provisional.

王纪华.note: A member of the Tuesday Dining Club and deputy leader of a comfort delegation; romanization provisional.

杨延修.note: 1912–2014; businessman and CCP underground figure, member of the Tuesday Dining Club.

顾执中.note: 1898–1995; journalist, leader of a comfort delegation to the New Fourth Army.

吴大琨.note: 1916–2007; economist, detained at Shangrao after leading a comfort delegation.

孙瑞璜.note: A financial-world member of the Tuesday Dining Club; romanization provisional.

王志莘.note: 1896–1957; banker, member of the Tuesday Dining Club.

吴耀宗.note: 1893–1979; Protestant leader, later a founder of the Three-Self Patriotic Movement.

王揆生.note: A Christian member of the Tuesday Dining Club who founded a remedial school; romanization provisional.

萧宗俊.note: A Christian member of the Tuesday Dining Club; romanization provisional.

陆高谊.note: A publishing-world member of the Tuesday Dining Club; romanization provisional.

姚惠泉.note: Representative of the Shanghai Local Association in the Tuesday Dining Club; romanization provisional.

李文杰.note: Lawyer and accountant, member of the Tuesday Dining Club, whom the author asked to write its memoir.

斯诺.note: Edgar Snow (1905–1972); American journalist, author of Red Star Over China.

朱立波.note: A comfort delegate to the New Fourth Army; romanization provisional.

顾祝同.note: 1893–1987; Kuomintang general, commander of the Third War Zone.

黄炎培.note: 1878–1965; educator, founder of the Chinese Vocational Education Society and of the China Democratic League.

胡鄂公.note: Style Nanhu; an early CCP member, later a counselor of the Nanjing Executive Yuan; romanization provisional.

孔祥熙.note: H. H. Kung (1881–1967); financier and premier, husband of Song Ailing.

孔令侃.note: 1916–1992; eldest son of Kong Xiangxi and Song Ailing.

朱学范.note: 1905–1996; labor-union leader and Du Yuesheng disciple; first PRC Minister of Posts and Telecommunications, later chairman of the Revolutionary Committee of the Kuomintang.

杜维藩.note: Eldest son of Du Yuesheng; romanization provisional.

姚玉兰.note: A wife of Du Yuesheng, a former Peking-opera actress; romanization provisional.

李芳.note: An old Northern Expedition comrade at whose Hong Kong home the author lodged; romanization provisional.

赵老太太.note: A patriotic old mother from the Northeast, the ‘mother of the guerrillas,’ who lost four sons in the war and sent the youngest to the front.

何东.note: 1862–1956; Eurasian Hong Kong businessman and philanthropist.

张曼怡.note: Given by the memoir as the wife of T. V. Soong; romanization provisional (some sources give his wife’s name as Zhang Leyi).

宋子文.note: 1894–1971; financier and statesman, brother of the Soong sisters.

胡汉民.note: 1879–1936; a leading Kuomintang theorist and rival of Chiang Kai-shek.

胡木兰.note: Daughter of Hu Hanmin, head of the Hong Kong Women’s Comfort Association; romanization provisional.

吴菊芳.note: Wife of General Li Hanhun, leader of a northbound comfort delegation; romanization provisional.

侯外庐.note: 1903–1987; Marxist historian, then engaged in intelligence work.

吴蕴初.note: 1891–1953; industrial chemist, China’s ‘MSG king,’ founder of the Tianchu factory.

戴女士.note: Wife of the industrialist Wu Yunchu; a co-founder of the Chinese Women’s Vocational School.

郭箴一.note: An underground Party member hidden at the Chinese Women’s Vocational School; romanization provisional.

蔡夏莹.note: An underground Party member hidden at the Chinese Women’s Vocational School; romanization provisional.

罗青长.note: 1918–2014; CCP intelligence official, co-author of the memorial article on Liu Shaowen.

柴成文.note: 1915–2011; PLA officer and diplomat, co-author of the memorial article on Liu Shaowen.

龚普生.note: 1913–2007; diplomat, deputy general secretary of the Shanghai YWCA.

国民党.note: Rendered ‘Kuomintang’ throughout (not ‘Nationalist Party’); the conventional English name.

粤汉铁路.note: Conventional English form of the Guangzhou–Hankou line.

互济会.note: Successor to the China Relief Society; the Party-led body for rescuing arrested comrades and relieving their families. Its leading arm is called the Mutual Aid General Association (互济总会).

世界与中国社.note: A progressive study body organized under the CCP Central Propaganda Department, publisher of the periodical The World and China.

内外棉.note: Naigaiwata Kaisha, the largest Japanese-owned cotton-spinning company in Shanghai; the author worked as an apprentice in its No. 13 Mill.

特科.note: The Central Special Branch, the Party’s clandestine intelligence and security service in Shanghai, headed by Zhou Enlai.

觉悟社.note: A progressive youth group founded in Tianjin in 1919; Zhou Enlai was a leading member, and his code name there, ‘Wu Hao’, later became a pen name.

中央特科.note: The CCP’s clandestine security and intelligence organ in the Shanghai underground; run by Kang Sheng after Gu Shunzhang’s defection.

红旗印刷所.note: The underground printing house, holding an open business licence, where the Party magazine Red Flag was secretly printed; wrecked by the police when Xiang Zhongfa turned traitor.

都城饭店.note: A French-run hotel in Shanghai (the Metropole, on Jiangxi Road), used by the central leaders as a bolt-hole on the night of Xiang Zhongfa’s defection.

东方饭店.note: A Shanghai hotel where Guan Xiangying was lodged after his release.

申江医院.note: An underground-Party hospital on Avenue Joffre, run by Party comrades, used to treat leaders and shelter them; the author hid there after her father’s death.

大光明电影院.note: A famous Shanghai cinema (the Grand Theatre).

永安公司.note: A leading Shanghai department store on Nanjing Road (Wing On).

祥生公司.note: A Shanghai taxi company (its English name was Johnson & Co.).

徐汇公学.note: The Jesuit Collège Saint-Ignace at Xujiahui, Shanghai; a strict Catholic mission school where Chen Zhigao and Cao Bingsheng were classmates.

锦江饭店.note: Dong Zhujun’s restaurant, later hotel, in Shanghai.

梅龙镇酒家.note: A well-known Shanghai restaurant run by Wu Mei.

中法药科大学.note: A Shanghai pharmacy college where Chen Baozhang studied.

十九路军.note: The Kuomintang army that resisted the Japanese attack on Shanghai in the January Twenty-eighth (1932) war.

华侨日报.note: A Chinese-language newspaper published in New York (the China Daily News).

永业银行.note: A Shanghai bank on Jiangxi Road whose porter’s lodge housed the World and China Society’s distribution office.

震旦大学.note: The French Jesuit Université l’Aurore in Shanghai, alma mater of Chen Zhigao and his circle.

暨南大学.note: Overseas-Chinese university in Shanghai where Chen Gaoyong was a professor.

通易信托公司.note: Shanghai trust company that went bankrupt in 1935 and, through the author and Chen Zhigao’s mediation, uniquely resumed business; it became a covert base for the underground.

银行俱乐部.note: A Shanghai club of the banking elite, which the author joined as one of its rare women members.

上海市银钱业联谊会.en: Shanghai Banking and Money Trades Friendship Association
上海市银钱业联谊会.note: A 1936 association of Shanghai’s banking and money-house trades; the author was a founder and deputy chairman.

风雨书屋.note: A covert resistance publishing house run by A Ying, hidden on the second floor of the Tongyi Company.

南社.note: An early-twentieth-century revolutionary poetry society; formally re-legalized in 1936 with help from the author’s circle.

救国会.note: The 1936 all-China resistance body whose leaders (the ‘Seven Gentlemen,’ among them Shen Junru) were jailed.

民权保障同盟.en: League for the Protection of Civil Rights
民权保障同盟.note: The China League for the Protection of Civil Rights (1932–33), which set up a committee to rescue political prisoners.

上海律师公会.note: The lawyers’ association through which Chen Zhigao and Shen Junru pressed the wrongful-imprisonment-compensation movement.

浙江兴业银行.note: The bank that took the mortgage on the Tongyi building, freeing the cash to pay small creditors.

交通银行.note: A major Chinese bank, cited as one that could not resume after bankruptcy, unlike Tongyi.

中华学艺社.en: Chinese Society for Arts and Sciences
中华学艺社.note: The Shanghai learned society at whose hall the author and Chen Zhigao held their 1935 wedding.

永昌金号.note: A gold exchange organized c.1933–34 by Chen Zhigao’s eldest brother, used to stand surety for released prisoners.

太极银号.note: A money house opened by the same circle, likewise used as surety for the rescue work.

八路军驻沪办事处.note: The Eighth Route Army’s liaison office in Shanghai, abbreviated ‘ba ban,’ which led the resistance periodical Documents.

民社党.note: The memoir's 民社党; in the mid-1930s the party of Zhang Junmai and Zhang Dongsun was the China National Socialist Party (国家社会党, founded 1932), which merged into the Democratic Socialist Party (民社党) only in 1946. Rendered by the party these figures belonged to at the time; unrelated to European fascism.

全国各界救国联合会.note: The national salvation-movement coalition led by Song Qingling; the ‘Salvation Association’ of these chapters.

中国民权保障同盟.en: China League for the Protection of Civil Rights
中国民权保障同盟.note: Founded by Song Qingling in Shanghai (Dec. 1932) to oppose arbitrary arrests and rescue political prisoners.

妇慰会.note: Short for the Shanghai Branch of the Chinese Women’s Association for the Comfort of the Officers and Men Defending the Country and Resisting the Enemy, headed by He Xiangning.

妇救会.note: The renamed Women’s Comfort Association; also rendered the Women’s Relief Association where the source varies (妇女救济会).

抗敌后援会.en: Association for the Support of Resistance to the Enemy
抗敌后援会.note: The Shanghai All-Circles Association for the Support of Resistance to the Enemy, a Kuomintang-led wartime body.

国际救济会.note: The Shanghai relief body founded through Father Rao (Jacquinot), running the International refugee shelters.

慈联会.note: Short for the Shanghai Federation of Charitable Bodies for United Relief, represented by Zhao Puchu.

星二聚餐会.note: A standing weekly gathering of Shanghai intellectuals and notables, a united-front ‘three-thirds’ experiment.

星五聚餐会.note: The Chongqing counterpart of the Tuesday Dining Club, led by the Eighth Route Office there.

卫国出版公司.note: A publishing company the author founded with Hong Kong funds to unify left-wing cultural supply in Shanghai.

中华女子职业学校.note: A women’s vocational school entrusted to the author, later turned (as the Chinese Vocational School) into a joint KMT–CCP intelligence-training front.

中华职业教育社.note: The vocational-education body founded by Huang Yanpei.

正大运输公司.note: A transport company opened within the Tongyi Company to keep the newspaper’s funds turning over.

反帝大同盟.note: An anti-imperialist mass organization; Wu Yaozong was a member.

复社.note: A left-wing publishing society (its name means ‘the Renaissance Society’) behind the Chinese edition of Red Star Over China.

大学图书公司.note: A British-registered Hong Kong firm whose name was used to publish the Daily Translation Herald.

民主同盟.note: The China Democratic League, an alliance of intermediate parties, dissolved by the Kuomintang in 1947.

上海市地方协会.note: A Shanghai civic body within Du Yuesheng’s sphere that helped fund the paper and schools.

文献.note: The resistance-and-salvation digest monthly edited by A Ying at the Wind and Rain Bookroom (1938).

译报.note: A short-lived 1937 concession paper of translated foreign dispatches, forerunner of the Daily Translation Herald.

每日译报.note: A CCP-backed ‘foreign-flag’ paper (1938) registered under British merchants to evade Japanese censorship; the author was its board chairman.

上海妇女.note: A women’s magazine that carried the author’s report and the Hong Kong group photograph.

人道报.note: The central organ of the French Communist Party, which dubbed the author the ‘Queen of the Refugees.’

大美晚报.note: An American-owned English/Chinese evening paper in Shanghai.

新闻报.note: Xinwen bao, a major old-established Shanghai commercial newspaper.

论持久战.note: Mao Zedong’s 1938 treatise, serialized by the Daily Translation Herald.

西行漫画.note: Huang Zhen’s album of Long March sketches, later reissued as the Long March Album (not to be confused with Snow’s Red Star Over China).

西行漫记.note: Edgar Snow’s 1937 reportage on the Yan’an base (literally ‘random notes on a journey to the west’).

碧血花.note: An anti-Japanese history play by A Ying, also titled Sorrow at the Fall of the Ming.

上海.note: China’s largest city and the seat of the Party Central and its underground in this period.

香港.note: British colony; seat of the Party’s Southern Bureau.

天津.note: North China treaty port; seat of the Party’s Northern Bureau.

龙华.note: District in the southern outskirts of Shanghai; site of the Kuomintang Garrison Command’s prison and execution ground.

庐山.note: A mountain resort in Jiangxi where Chiang Kai-shek was staying.

瑞金.note: The seat of the Central Soviet in Jiangxi, capital of the Chinese Soviet Republic.

大连.note: A city in Liaoning; Guan Xiangying’s native region, site of his memorial statue.

延安.note: The Communist base in northern Shaanxi from 1937.

霞飞路.note: A main thoroughfare of the Shanghai French Concession, today’s Central Huaihai Road.

法大马路.note: A street in the Shanghai French Concession, today’s Jinling East Road; the address on the counter-notice.

杭州.note: Zhejiang provincial capital on West Lake, where the author went into hiding in 1932–33.

西湖.note: The famous scenic lake of Hangzhou around which this chapter is set.

孤山.note: An islet-hill in West Lake beside which the Yu Mansion stands.

俞楼.note: The three-story Yu family villa by Solitary Hill where the author lodged and studied poetry.

虎跑寺.note: A Hangzhou temple, also called Dinghui Temple, whose name the author took as Huang Dinghui.

烟霞洞.note: A grotto near West Lake bearing the ‘Xiangxiang’ rock inscription left by Chen Zhigao’s party.

灵隐寺.note: A major Buddhist temple by West Lake where the author’s mother made her vow.

北平.note: The name of Beijing under the Nationalist government (1928–49); site of the Tongyi Company’s largest creditors.

苏州.note: Jiangsu city, site of the Second Jiangsu Prison and of the wrongful-imprisonment-compensation meetings.

南京.note: The Nationalist capital in this period.

青岛.note: Shandong port city, host of the Fifth National Bar Association congress (1933).

珞珈山.note: The Wuhan University campus hill where the author met Guo Changlu.

东交民巷.note: The Legation Quarter of Beiping, most of whose land the Tongyi branch held.

西天目.note: A mountain in Zhejiang where the author and Chen Zhigao honeymooned and planted plum trees.

柳林.note: He Chang’s home county in Shanxi, site of his memorial hall.

会昌.note: The south Jiangxi county at whose river He Chang was ambushed and killed in 1935.

绥远.note: A former province of Inner Mongolia, focus of a 1936 resistance campaign.

大千世界.note: A Shanghai amusement hall where benefit performances were held.

兰心大戏院.note: A well-known theater in the Shanghai French Concession.

新光大戏院.note: A Shanghai theater where wartime benefit operas were staged.

沧州饭店.note: A Shanghai hotel where Guo Moruo was lodged on his return.

金巴利道.note: A road in Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon, Hong Kong.

思豪酒家.note: A Hong Kong restaurant where the welcome for Old Madame Zhao was held; romanization provisional.

华东医院.note: A Shanghai hospital where the author was later visited.

上饶集中营.note: A Kuomintang camp in Jiangxi where captured resistance figures were held.

南市.note: The old South City district of Shanghai, site of the Nanshi Refugee Zone.

秀才.note: Lowest degree-holder of the imperial examinations; left romanized.

优贡.note: ‘Excellent tribute student,’ a special examination distinction; left romanized.

临江仙.note: ‘The Immortal by the River,’ a fixed ci lyric-pattern; each part of the book opens with one.

伍豪.note: An alias of Zhou Enlai, from his code name in the Awakening Society; the pivot of the fake ‘renunciation’ notices and their rebuttal.

周公.note: An honorific for Zhou Enlai; literally ‘Duke of Zhou’, the revered Zhou-dynasty statesman, here used as a byname of respect.

太史公.note: An honorific for a former Hanlin compiler/historian; used of Yu Biyun throughout this chapter.

破产法.note: The Republican bankruptcy statute whose three-quarters-of-creditors rule shaped the Tongyi mediation.

反省院.note: A Nationalist ‘Three People’s Principles’ re-education facility to which unconvicted political prisoners could be transferred, used as a rescue channel.

白区.note: Kuomintang-controlled territory, as opposed to the Red (soviet) areas; the author’s underground post was in the Shanghai white area.

孤岛.note: The Shanghai foreign concessions after Nov. 1937, surrounded by Japanese-held territory until Dec. 1941.

三三制.note: The CCP united-front formula sharing places among Communists, non-Party progressives, and centrists.
